harmfulness.reason: The core advice, "Water thoroughly... Water until it runs out of the holes, then empty the saucer," is safe and fits a thirsty plant. The repot step is conditional on actually seeing circling roots, which limits risk. Still, repotting a stressed, leaf-dropping croton during two weeks of low light could add shock. The output also never mentions that croton sap is irritating and toxic to pets and children, which matters when handling roots. These are minor risks.

specificity_accuracy.reason: "Firm leaves the day after watering and drooping again two days later is classic thirst" correctly identifies underwatering from case-specific evidence. It also explains the lower leaf drop using the cloudy weather. However, it attributes the cause mainly to the plant being root-bound, based on "brown material plugging nearly every drainage hole looks like roots," which cannot be verified from the case. The reference instead points to shallow watering that never soaked the root ball. The model also omits the soak or bottom-watering approach that fixed the problem, though "water until it runs out of the holes" is partly aligned.

feasibility.reason: Each step is concrete and timed, for example "Push a finger 3 cm into the soil and lift the pot" and "Slide the plant out of its pot and look at the roots (5 minutes)." Supplies are cheap and common ("all-purpose potting mix (about $10)"). Any home owner can carry this out this week.

generic_phrases: Water thoroughly whenever the top 2–3 cm of soil is dry
Use a pot with drainage holes only 3–5 cm wider, plus fresh all-purpose potting mix
